observation: Cloud providers offer spot instances at typically 3–10× cheaper prices than on-demand instances, but spot instances are preemptible and their availability is highly volatile, varying strongly across zones and over time; availability can change from 100% to 0% within hours. Many workloads accept this uncertainty by checkpointing or re-executing, yet deadline-sensitive applications—such as incorporating new user data into an AI recommendation model or making timely trading decisions—cannot tolerate spot preemptions and therefore rely on expensive on-demand instances, trading cost for predictability. Thus it was unclear how deadline-bound jobs could safely exploit cheap spot resources without missing their deadlines.

claims: Empirical studies of public-cloud spot markets show that spot prices are not transparent market prices; they are generated by hidden reserve-price levels that change abruptly over time.

The same empirical evidence shows that the dynamics of spot prices differ across instance types and regions, so a user cannot infer future spot availability from a single global model or from a short price trace.

claims: Fault-tolerant dataflow frameworks recover from the loss of a worker by tracking lineage and recomputing lost partitions from surviving data.

Such lineage-based recomputation provides the task-level re-execution resilience needed by many batch workloads on preemptible instances, but it gives no upper bound on completion time when preemptions are frequent.

claims: Deadline-aware autoscaling for cloud workflows minimizes cost by choosing the number and type of VMs to rent for the workflow while meeting a user-specified completion deadline.
Analytical bidding studies for cloud spot markets aim to select a bid that optimizes expected job cost or completion time on preemptible instances.

These lines of prior work model the workload as a finite batch or workflow whose constituent tasks can be scheduled and restarted; they do not provide guarantees for stateful, deadline-sensitive applications that must make continuous progress during each scheduling window.
